quotes.text: Emerging from the 1960s British blues scene, the band soon developed a distinctive progressive rock sound, blending hard rock, English folk music and classical music, while undergoing numerous stylistic shifts throughout its history.

After a key lineup change which saw original guitarist Mick Abrahams replaced by Barre, the band achieved their first major success the following year with their folk-influenced second album Stand Up.

Aqualung (1971) marked the band's international breakthrough and became their most commercially successful album, while subsequent releases such as Thick as a Brick (1972) fully established their progressive rock identity.

Throughout the 1970s the band maintained an intense schedule of touring and recording, releasing one studio album every year and expanding their musical scope through concept albums and increasingly complex arrangements.
In the late 1970s the band shifted towards folk rock, before a major lineup change led to a period influenced by electronic rock in the early 1980s.
The band returned to a hard rock sound with Crest of a Knave (1987), which earned them their only Grammy Award, and explored world music influences in the 1990s.
Living in the Past is loaded with some amazing work during the period covering Tull's transformation from a blues-jazz combo to a multi-faceted ensemble capable of excellence in a range of genres.

What I love most about Living in the Past is that it's a showcase for the diversity of Ian Anderson's songwriting. I've always likened Ian to a restless butterfly, constantly searching for new topics to explore and new sounds to savor, and Living in the Past encapsulates that glorious restlessness.

If you could pick one song that served as the transition song par excellence to Stand Up, it would be this one. The song opens with Ian playing a folkish arpeggio on the mandolin; the band's entry is heralded by a brief flute run that triggers a rocking 4/4 beat with the electric guitar providing contra-rhythms.

Tull defies expectations with a triple shift—musical (chord pattern change marked by Mick Abraham's wah-wah chords), rhythmic (the band backs off the straight drive and introduces new contra-rhythms) and lyrical.

Tull has made a lot of great albums over the years – but none since Heavy Horses by my reckoning. At 77 years old, is it even fair to expect a classic album out of Ian Anderson? I say yes. I'm not willing to lower my expectations when I know what an artist is capable of, even if they haven't delivered a classic in almost five decades. It is Ian himself who set the bar I measure all Jethro Tull albums against, after all.
Curious Ruminant is as good an example as any of what has gone wrong with Tull for what is now three times as long as anything went right.

First, I think Ian is proud of writing impenetrable lyrics that mean nothing to anyone but him. He started on that kick on Thick as a Brick a bit, dove headfirst into it for A Passion Play, pulled back a bit for a couple of albums, and then pretty much decided if no one else besides him on the planet was smart enough to know what his lyrics meant, then the rest of the world needed to stop being so stupid.

I am all for thoughtful lyrics, I am even completely on board with challenging lyrics – but lyrics have to be at least the teeniest bit relatable to somebody besides the person who wrote them to really work, and Ian hasn't managed that in years.

He likes to pepper his lyrics with big words and awkwardly constructed phrases that are more about showing off his vocabulary than sharing an idea that resonates with another human being. For decades now his lyrics have all been Ian-centric word salad.

Second, I feel kind of bad for picking on him about his vocal limitations, but the limited range of his voice in fact restricts the range of his melodies, which is a big part of the reason they come out sounding all samey.
And because he can't sing more than about five notes, all of his melodies have to fit in that range.
Third, Tull has always at times had an unfortunate propensity towards music that is more busy than musical.

"Puppet and the Puppet Master" begins with a lovely bit of piano, which sounded promising for all of about three seconds, but then the band starts projectile vomiting notes at us in a manner that is technically impressive but not artistically enjoyable.

"Stygian Hand" is another example of Ian spraying us with a firehose torrent of notes that, again, I have no doubt requires quite a bit of technical skill to play, but isn't a whole lot of fun to listen to.
But fifth and most crucially, like about every Jethro Tull album released since 1978, there just aren't a lot of good songs.
The album consists of a single continuous piece of music, split across the two sides of the original LP record, and was conceived as a parody of concept albums and the progressive rock genre.

Musically, Thick as a Brick features an intricate suite of progressive rock, characterized by complex musical structures and frequent time signature changes, incorporating elements of art rock, folk and classical music.

The album's lyrics draw partly on Anderson's childhood experiences and explore coming of age themes including conformity and intergenerational conflict, reflecting anti-establishment perspectives on institutions and authority.
Anderson began to write a piece that would combine complex music with a sense of humour, with the idea it would poke light-hearted fun at the band, the audience, and the music critics.
He also intended to satirise the progressive rock genre that was popular at the time.

Anderson has also said that "the album was a spoof to the albums of Yes and Emerson, Lake & Palmer, much like what the movie Airplane! had been to Airport" and later remarked that it was a "bit of a satire about the whole concept of grand rock-based concept albums".

Unlike previous albums, where Anderson had generally written songs in advance, only the initial section of the album had been worked out when the band went into the studio. The remainder of the suite was written during the recording sessions.
The lyrics were written first, with the music constructed to fit around them.
Guitarist Martin Barre recalls the whole band coming up with various ideas for the music.
Some parts were recorded in a single take with every member having an input, including significant contributions from keyboardist John Evan.
If Aqualung doubled down on the "concept album" concept, Thick as a Brick functioned as a New Testament of sorts, signifying what was now possible in rock music.
